22.0.big: Prokaryotes (Bacteria and Archaea) are everywhere: in soil, water, extreme places, and on and inside you. Most are harmless or helpful.
points: There are about 10 times more bacterial cells in and on your body than human cells. Many help with digestion and protection.

22.1.big: Prokaryotes were Earth's first life, about 3.5 billion years ago, and they can live almost anywhere, even in extreme places.
points: Early Earth had no oxygen (it was anoxic), strong radiation (no ozone layer), lots of volcanoes and quakes. The first life was anaerobic.
Microbial mats (layered sheets of prokaryotes) may be the earliest life, possibly around hydrothermal vents. Stromatolites are their fossilized layers.
Cyanobacteria evolved photosynthesis that releases oxygen, which slowly filled the atmosphere and made aerobic life possible.

Extremophiles love extreme conditions: acidophiles (pH 3 or below), alkaliphiles (pH 9+), thermophiles (60–80 °C), hyperthermophiles (80–122 °C), psychrophiles (cold, −15 to 10 °C), halophiles (salty, like the Dead Sea), osmophiles (high sugar), and radioresistant types.

Over 99% of prokaryotes can't be grown in a lab. Some are alive but in a viable-but-non-culturable (VBNC) state; they may come back to life later (resuscitation). Scientists detect them with DNA tools like PCR instead.
Biofilms are communities of microbes glued together on a surface by a slimy matrix (like dental plaque). They're much harder to kill than single cells.

22.2.big: A prokaryote is a simple cell: no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles, but it has everything needed to live.
points: Every cell has a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA, and ribosomes. Prokaryotes keep their circular DNA in a nucleoid region, not a nucleus, and often carry extra plasmids.
Shapes: cocci (round), bacilli (rods), spirilli (spirals).
Extras: a capsule (sticky protective coat), flagella (swimming), a pilus (attachment and passing DNA), and an S-layer (protein layer).
Bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan. Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan wall with teichoic acid (stains purple). Gram-negative: thin wall plus an outer membrane (stains pink).
Archaea have pseudopeptidoglycan (or none) in their walls, and their membranes use different lipids (phytanyl groups instead of fatty acids).
Reproduction is by binary fission (copying). New genes come in by transformation (picking up DNA), transduction (a virus carries it), and conjugation (DNA passed through a pilus).
22.2.tip: Gram positive = purple = thick Peptidoglycan. Gram negative = pink = thin wall + outer membrane.

22.3.big: Prokaryotes get energy and carbon in every possible way, and they keep Earth's carbon and nitrogen cycles running.
points: A nutrient is anything needed to live. Macronutrients (needed a lot): C, H, O, N, P, S. Carbon is about 50% of a cell. Micronutrients (small amounts): iron, manganese, boron, and others.
Energy: phototrophs use light. Chemotrophs use chemicals.
Carbon: autotrophs fix CO₂. Heterotrophs get carbon from organic compounds. Combine them: chemoheterotroph, photoautotroph, and so on.
Carbon cycle: prokaryotes are decomposers that return CO₂ to the air.

Nitrogen cycle, all done by prokaryotes: nitrogen fixation (N₂ gas → ammonia, which plants and animals can use), ammonification (dead stuff → ammonia), nitrification (ammonia → nitrite → nitrate), denitrification (nitrate → N₂ gas back to the air).
22.3.tip: Photo/chemo = where energy comes from. Auto/hetero = where carbon comes from.

22.4.big: A few bacteria cause serious disease, and antibiotic resistance is making them harder to treat.
points: Disease words: epidemic (many cases at once), pandemic (worldwide epidemic), endemic disease (always around, usually at low levels), emerging disease (new, or suddenly rising).

History: the Plague of Athens (likely typhoid), the Black Death (bubonic plague from Yersinia pestis, spread by fleas on rats; it killed about half of Europe). A zoonosis is a disease that jumps from animals to people.
Biofilms cause problems on teeth (plaque), medical devices, wounds and food equipment.
Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses. Overuse (for colds and in livestock feed) selects for resistant superbugs like MRSA and community-acquired CA-MRSA.
Foodborne disease: E. coli, Salmonella, botulism (toxin from Clostridium, whose spores survive heat). Different strains of one species are called serotypes.

22.5.big: Most prokaryotes help us: they fertilize soil, make food, and clean up pollution.
points: Biological nitrogen fixation: Rhizobia live in root nodules of legumes (beans, peas). The plant gets nitrogen, the bacteria get sugars, and the soil gets fertilized. That's symbiosis.
Biotechnology started with microbes: cheese, yogurt, and bread (yeast). Fermentation also kept food from spoiling.
Bioremediation: microbes break down pollutants like oil spills (Exxon Valdez), pesticides and industrial waste. Success depends on the type of oil, the right microbes, and temperature.

1.why: Fossil microbial mats date back about 3.5 billion years.

2.why: False: early Earth had lots of geologic upheaval and volcanoes.

4.why: A normal drought is a moderate condition. Some bacteria survive it as spores.

6.why: We simply don't know what most of them need to grow.

7.why: Microbial mats may be the earliest life. Stromatolites are their fossils.

8.why: Different atmosphere, strong radiation, and lots of geologic and volcanic activity.

9.why: Halophiles need salt of at least 0.2 M.

12.why: False: their cell walls differ (peptidoglycan vs. pseudopeptidoglycan).

14.why: The cell wall is outside the cell membrane.

15.why: Sulfur is a macronutrient (needed in large amounts). Boron, manganese and iron are micronutrients.

16.why: False: iron is a micronutrient, needed only in small amounts.

18.why: Organic compounds for both energy and carbon = chemoorganotrophs (chemoheterotrophs).

19.why: They're decomposers that return carbon to the air.

20.why: Ammonification = decomposers release ammonia from dead organic matter.

21.why: Phosphorus is a macronutrient (in DNA, ATP, membranes).

23.why: Plague, diphtheria and cholera are bacterial. Yellow fever and dengue are viral.

25.why: False: biofilms do form in wounds, burns and devices like pacemakers.

26.why: Bacteria are becoming resistant to our antibiotics.

27.why: False: patients' ages have nothing to do with resistance. Overuse is the cause.

28.why: False: endemic diseases are usually at low incidence, not high.

29.why: Eukaryotes can't use N₂ gas, so it must be converted to ammonia.

30.why: False: algae can't fix nitrogen. Only prokaryotes (like cyanobacteria), lightning, and industry can.

31.why: Cheese, yogurt and bread all rely on microbes.

32.why: Fermenting foods preserved their nutrients (kept them from spoiling).

34.why: False: ammonia in soil is a nutrient, not a pollutant to clean up.

36.why: No O₂ at first, so life was anaerobic. Phototrophs came within a billion years, then cyanobacteria, which made oxygen.

37.why: Their natural adaptations (like DNA repair in radiation-resistant species) can be put to work for us.

38.why: Detect them with molecular biology tools, and amplify their DNA with PCR.

39.why: Little oxygen, no ozone (strong radiation), and lots of volcanic activity: an extreme world for extremophiles.

40.why: Cell wall, membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and a nucleoid (no nucleus), plus optional capsule, flagellum, pili and plasmids.

41.why: Same parts. Bacteria have peptidoglycan walls and fatty acid membranes. Archaea have neither peptidoglycan nor fatty acids (they use phytanyl groups).

42.why: All three shapes have the same basic parts. Only the shape differs.

43.why: Carbon is in every macromolecule and makes up about 50% of a cell.

44.why: No light, so energy comes from chemicals (chemo). Carbon comes from an amino acid, which is organic (heterotroph). (Choices a and d are the same.)

45.why: You'd still need fruits and vegetables (for other nutrients) and water, but nitrogen could come straight from the air.

46.why: Both are essential. Micronutrients are just needed in smaller amounts.

47.why: Pick a time above the line. At 85 °C you need about 50–200 minutes, so 300 is safe. At 90 °C about 10–25 minutes, so 30 also works. At 70–75 °C you'd need hundreds or thousands of minutes.

48.why: Yes. Better canning cut botulism, and outbreaks now come mostly from large-scale food production.

49.why: Spores drop from about 10⁶ to about 10³ in the first ~10 minutes, so most die fast. A few survive much longer.

50.why: It was likely typhoid (Salmonella Typhi), which still causes 16–33 million cases and over 200,000 deaths a year.

51.why: Plants get endless nitrogen, the soil is fertilized, and the bacteria get sugars from the plant.

52.why: Every bacterium's mercury line rises (only the control stays flat), and most level off by day 3–4.

53.why: It depends on the type of oil, the oil-eating microbes present, and the temperature.

54.why: Rhizobia give plants nitrogen, and the plants give them sugars (photosynthates). Both benefit.

55.why: Bacteria stuck together in a polysaccharide matrix = a biofilm.

56.why: Without an energy source (like lightning), the molecules don't react. Early Earth must have had that energy.

57.why: At 45 °C, E. coli, Clostridium AK1 and Thermoanaerobacterium AK17 all show growth. AK15 starts near 48 °C and Paenibacillus stops near 35 °C.

58.why: Figure 22.10 shows a prokaryote: a bacterial cell.

59.why: Both have ribosomes, prokaryotes usually have walls (some eukaryotes too), and DNA is in a nucleoid vs. a nucleus.

60.why: False: binary fission only copies a cell. It doesn't move genes to a different bacterium.

61.why: Conjugation lets some cells get new gene combos, which helps in a changing environment.

62.why: On ampicillin, only resistant cells survive: plate IV.

63.why: Only some cells took up the plasmid, and only those survive ampicillin.

64.why: A loose circular DNA in a nucleoid (no nucleus) marks a prokaryote. Ribosomes, walls and cytoplasm also exist in eukaryotes.

65.why: Studying a new methanogen can show whether metabolic pathways evolved separately in Bacteria and Archaea.

66.why: It fixes the most nitrogen at 15 cm, the deepest level with the least oxygen, so it's probably anaerobic.

67.why: Know the pieces. Chemo = energy from chemicals. Auto = makes its own carbon compounds from CO₂. Hetero = takes carbon from organic food. Obligate anaerobes die in oxygen. Facultative anaerobes can live with or without it.

68.why: Strain 1 made more potassium available (uptake went up). Strain 2 made less available.

69.why: Plaque is bacteria stuck together on teeth: a biofilm.

70.why: It was contained after 1945, then cases shot up again: re-emerging.

71.why: The 20-year-old spores formed while the pollutant was present, so they're likely adapted to it and grow better.

72.why: 3GCRKP's bubble sits slightly right (more cases) and slightly lower (fewer deaths) than CRPA.

73.why: France has the highest penicillin use and the most resistance, so cutting back could help. The Netherlands is the low-use, low-resistance model.

74.why: The trend line goes up: more outpatient use, more resistance.

75.why: The productivity line is highest on the right, where fields use synthetic fertilizer (green bars).

76.why: The graph shows farmers switching from legumes to synthetic fertilizer, but not how efficient either one is. Usage trends alone can't prove efficiency.

77.why: Healthy-skin strains just eat oil (commensal). Acne strains cause harm (parasitic).
